Lab 1 · Predicting medical insurance charges, step by step¶

AI Foundations · Practical Lab 1 (revises Lessons 1–7)

In the lessons we learned why things work. In this lab we do it: one real problem, from a raw CSV file to a model we can save, explain and use.

Every step has three parts:

  1. What we do (the code)
  2. Why we do it (the reasoning)
  3. Revision box: which lesson the idea came from

How to use this notebook: run each cell in order with Shift + Enter. Read the text before running the code, and predict what will happen. Then check.

Step 1 · The problem¶

ACME Insurance wants to estimate the yearly medical charges of a new customer from 6 facts: age, sex, BMI, number of children, smoker or not, region. The estimate is used to set the customer's premium.

Two business rules shape everything we do:

  • Accuracy: a wrong estimate costs money (too low → losses, too high → the customer goes to a competitor).
  • Explainability: regulators require that we can explain why a customer got a certain estimate. A black box is not allowed.

What kind of ML problem is this?¶

  • We have past customers with the answer (their real charges) → supervised learning.
  • The answer is a number (dollars) → regression (not classification).

How will we measure success?¶

We will use RMSE (root mean squared error): roughly, "how many dollars off are we, typically, with big misses punished more". We will also report MAE (mean absolute error: the plain average miss in dollars) and R² (the share of variation we explain: 0 = useless, 1 = perfect).

📘 Revision (Lesson 1): ML = learning a rule from examples instead of writing it by hand. Supervised = examples come with answers. Regression = the answer is a number.

We import the tools we need. Each library has one job:

  • pandas: tables · numpy: maths on arrays · matplotlib / seaborn: charts · scikit-learn: the ML models.

Finding: no missing values, but one customer appears twice, identical in every column.

Why does a duplicate matter? If one copy ends up in training and the other in testing, the model is tested on a customer it has already seen: a small leak that makes the score look better than reality. We remove it.

📘 Revision (Lesson 2 · leakage): anything that lets information from the test set sneak into training makes your score a lie.

Step 3 · Split the data before we look closely¶

This feels strange: why split before exploring? Because we are part of the model too. If we stare at all the data, notice patterns and design features from them, we have quietly used the test set. Then the test score is no longer an honest preview of new customers.

So: 20% goes into a locked box (test set), opened once, at the very end (Step 14).

random_state=42 makes the split repeatable: everyone in class gets the same rows.

📘 Revision (Lesson 2): train = learn, validation = choose, test = final honest check, used once.

In [6]:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

train_df, test_df = train_test_split(df, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)
print('Training customers:', len(train_df))
print('Test customers (locked away):', len(test_df))

Training customers: 1069
Test customers (locked away): 268

Step 4 · Explore the training data¶

Goal: understand what drives charges, so we can choose good features and a good model. Always ask: what does this chart tell me, and what should I do about it?

4.1 The target: how are charges distributed?¶

In [7]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4.5))
sns.histplot(train_df.charges, bins=50, ax=ax[0], color='steelblue')
ax[0].set_title('Annual medical charges')
sns.histplot(data=train_df, x='charges', hue='smoker', bins=50, ax=ax[1], palette={'no':'grey','yes':'crimson'})
ax[1].set_title('Charges: smokers vs non-smokers')
plt.show()

print(train_df.groupby('smoker').charges.median().rename('median charges'))
print('Share of smokers:', round((train_df.smoker == 'yes').mean() * 100, 1), '%')

smoker
no     7,348.14
yes   33,391.68
Name: median charges, dtype: float64
Share of smokers: 20.0 %

What we learn:

  • Most customers pay under $15,000; a few pay $40,000+ (the skewed tail).
  • Smoking is huge: the median smoker costs about 4.5× a non-smoker (~$33,000 vs ~$7,300). Only 1 in 5 customers smokes, but they are most of the expensive tail.

4.2 Age vs charges¶

In [8]:
sns.scatterplot(data=train_df, x='age', y='charges', hue='smoker', palette={'no':'grey','yes':'crimson'}, s=25, alpha=.8)
plt.title('Age vs charges'); plt.show()

What we learn: three bands, each rising with age:

  1. bottom band: mostly healthy non-smokers
  2. middle band: a mix (non-smokers with health problems + some smokers)
  3. top band: only smokers

Charges rise steadily with age in every band, and the rise looks slightly curved (steeper for older people). Remember that curve.

📘 Revision (Lesson 7): we just "clustered" by eye: groups that nobody labelled. Spotting structure like this guides our model choices.

4.3 BMI vs charges: the most important chart in this lab¶

In [9]:
sns.scatterplot(data=train_df, x='bmi', y='charges', hue='smoker', palette={'no':'grey','yes':'crimson'}, s=25, alpha=.8)
plt.axvline(30, color='black', ls='--'); plt.text(30.5, 60000, 'BMI 30 = obesity line')
plt.title('BMI vs charges'); plt.show()

Look carefully. For non-smokers (grey), BMI barely matters. For smokers (red), there is a jump at BMI 30: smokers who are obese cost far more.

This is called an interaction: the effect of one feature (BMI) depends on another feature (smoking). A plain linear model cannot see this on its own; it gives BMI one fixed weight for everybody. We will come back to this in Step 10.

4.4 Correlation: a number for "how linearly related"¶

In [10]:
corr_df = train_df.assign(smoker_yes=(train_df.smoker == 'yes').astype(int),
                          male=(train_df.sex == 'male').astype(int))
corr = corr_df[['age', 'bmi', 'children', 'smoker_yes', 'male', 'charges']].corr()
sns.heatmap(corr, annot=True, fmt='.2f', cmap='Reds', vmin=-1, vmax=1)
plt.title('Correlation matrix (training data)'); plt.show()

Reading it: correlation runs from −1 to +1. With charges: smoker 0.77 (strong), age 0.29, BMI 0.18, children 0.09, sex ≈ 0.

Two warnings:

  1. Correlation ≠ causation. Correlation says two things move together, not that one causes the other.
  2. Correlation only measures straight-line relationships. BMI's correlation looks weak (0.18), yet for smokers BMI is critical. Weak correlation does not mean useless.

Step 5 · The baseline: the dumbest possible model¶

Before building anything clever, ask: what score do we get with no intelligence at all? The dumbest regression model predicts the same number for everyone: the average training charge.

Why bother? Without a baseline, a number like "RMSE 6,000" means nothing. Is that good? Compared to what? The baseline is the floor every real model must beat.

📘 Revision (Lessons 3, 6): in Lesson 3 the baseline was "predict nobody churns" (73.5% accuracy!). In Lesson 6 we saw that fancy boosting beat logistic regression by only 0.008 AUC. Always compare against something simple.

In [11]:
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error, mean_absolute_error, r2_score

def rmse(y_true, y_pred):
    return np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred))

baseline_value = train_df.charges.mean()
print(f'Baseline predicts ${baseline_value:,.0f} for every customer')
# we peek at the test set ONLY for this baseline, to set expectations; we never tune on it
print(f'Baseline RMSE on training data: ${rmse(train_df.charges, np.full(len(train_df), baseline_value)):,.0f}')

Baseline predicts $13,030 for every customer
Baseline RMSE on training data: $11,701

Result: about $12,000 typical error. Any model we build must do clearly better than this.

Step 6 · One feature, one straight line¶

Let's start tiny, so we can see every moving part. Take non-smokers only and predict charges from age with a straight line:

$$\text{charges} = w \times \text{age} + b$$

  • w (weight / slope): how many extra dollars per year of age
  • b (bias / intercept): where the line starts

Training = finding the best w and b. We will do it three ways, as in Lesson 4.

In [12]:
non_smokers = train_df[train_df.smoker == 'no']
ages = non_smokers.age.values
targets = non_smokers.charges.values

def try_parameters(w, b):
    predictions = w * ages + b
    plt.scatter(ages, targets, s=10, alpha=.6, label='actual')
    plt.plot(ages, predictions, 'r', label=f'line: w={w:.0f}, b={b:.0f}')
    plt.xlabel('age'); plt.ylabel('charges'); plt.legend()
    plt.title(f'RMSE = ${rmse(targets, predictions):,.0f}')
    plt.show()

Way 1: guess by hand¶

Try a guess. Then change w and b yourself and watch the RMSE. Exercise: can you get below $5,000?

In [13]:
try_parameters(w=50, b=100)
In [14]:
try_parameters(w=150, b=1000)

Guessing works, but slowly. We need two things to automate it:

  1. A loss function that scores a line with one number (we have it: RMSE / MSE).
  2. An optimizer that changes w and b to reduce the loss.

Way 2: gradient descent from scratch (Lesson 4)¶

The recipe: compute the slope of the loss for w and b (the gradient), take a small step downhill, repeat.

We scale age first (subtract mean, divide by standard deviation). Why? In Lesson 4, scaling cut gradient descent from 53,586 steps to 16. Unscaled, w and b live on very different scales and the descent zig-zags.

In [15]:
x = (ages - ages.mean()) / ages.std()     # scaled age
y = targets
w, b = 0.0, 0.0                           # start anywhere
learning_rate = 0.1
history = []

for step in range(300):
    predictions = w * x + b
    error = predictions - y
    grad_w = 2 * np.mean(error * x)       # slope of MSE with respect to w
    grad_b = 2 * np.mean(error)           # slope of MSE with respect to b
    w -= learning_rate * grad_w           # step downhill
    b -= learning_rate * grad_b
    history.append(rmse(y, predictions))

plt.plot(history); plt.xlabel('step'); plt.ylabel('RMSE'); plt.title('Gradient descent: loss going down'); plt.show()

# convert back from scaled age to real age
w_real = w / ages.std()
b_real = b - w * ages.mean() / ages.std()
print(f'Gradient descent found: w = {w_real:.2f}, b = {b_real:.2f}')

Gradient descent found: w = 264.98, b = -1960.57

Way 3: let scikit-learn solve it exactly¶

LinearRegression uses a direct mathematical solution (least squares), no steps needed. For small linear problems this is the best choice.

In [16]:
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

line = LinearRegression().fit(non_smokers[['age']], non_smokers.charges)   # note: X must be 2-D, hence [['age']]
print(f'scikit-learn found:       w = {line.coef_[0]:.2f}, b = {line.intercept_:.2f}')
try_parameters(line.coef_[0], line.intercept_)

scikit-learn found:       w = 264.98, b = -1960.57

Both methods agree to the cent: about $265 more per year of age. Gradient descent gets there step by step; the formula jumps there directly.

Why does the line sit above most dots? The few expensive non-smokers (the middle band) pull it up. Squared error punishes big misses heavily, so the line compromises toward them.

📘 Revision (Lesson 4): model + loss + optimizer = machine learning. Gradient descent scales to billions of parameters (that is how LLMs train); the direct formula is best for small linear problems.

Step 7 · All features: encoding, scaling and a pipeline¶

Models only understand numbers. Three columns are text: sex, smoker, region. How to convert them?

Option How When to use
Label numbers (northeast=0, northwest=1, …) one column of integers ❌ for regions: it invents an order (is southwest "3× northwest"?)
Binary 0/1 yes → 1, no → 0 ✅ two categories (smoker, sex)
One-hot encoding one 0/1 column per category ✅ few categories with no order (region)
Ordinal keep the natural order (low < medium < high) ✅ ordered categories
Target / frequency encoding replace category by a statistic many categories (e.g. 1,000 cities); careful with leakage

Best choice here: one-hot encoding with drop='first'. Why drop one column? The 4 region columns always add up to 1, so one is redundant (if you're not NE, NW or SE, you're SW). With a linear model, this redundancy (the "dummy variable trap") makes the weights unstable and hard to read.

Why a pipeline?¶

We could encode and scale by hand, but production systems use a Pipeline: one object that does preprocessing and the model. Three reasons:

  1. No leakage: the scaler learns its mean/std from training folds only, automatically, even inside cross-validation.
  2. No mismatch: new customers get exactly the same transformation as training data.
  3. One file to save and deploy (Step 16).
In [17]:
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

numeric_cols = ['age', 'bmi', 'children']
categorical_cols = ['sex', 'smoker', 'region']

preprocess = ColumnTransformer([
    ('num', StandardScaler(), numeric_cols),
    ('cat', OneHotEncoder(drop='first', handle_unknown='ignore'), categorical_cols),
])

X_train = train_df.drop(columns='charges')
y_train = train_df.charges

linear_model = make_pipeline(preprocess, LinearRegression())
linear_model.fit(X_train, y_train)

# look inside: what columns did the preprocessing create?
print(linear_model[0].get_feature_names_out())

['num__age' 'num__bmi' 'num__children' 'cat__sex_male' 'cat__smoker_yes'
 'cat__region_northwest' 'cat__region_southeast' 'cat__region_southwest']

Let's read the weights. Because numeric features are scaled, their weights are comparable: "dollars per one standard deviation". Binary weights mean "dollars for having this category".

In [18]:
weights = pd.Series(linear_model[-1].coef_, index=linear_model[0].get_feature_names_out()).sort_values()
weights.plot.barh(color=['crimson' if v < 0 else 'steelblue' for v in weights])
plt.title('Linear model weights ($)'); plt.show()
print('Intercept (base charge):', round(linear_model[-1].intercept_))
weights.round(0)

Intercept (base charge): 8948
Out[18]:
cat__region_southeast     -839.00
cat__region_southwest     -659.00
cat__region_northwest     -392.00
cat__sex_male             -102.00
num__children              637.00
num__bmi                 1,928.00
num__age                 3,473.00
cat__smoker_yes         23,078.00

Reading the model: being a smoker adds about $23,000. Age (one standard deviation ≈ 14 years) adds ~$3,500. BMI ~$1,900. Sex and region matter little.

📘 Revision (Lesson 4): compare weights only after scaling; otherwise a feature measured in big units gets a tiny weight and looks unimportant.

Step 8 · Cross-validation: a fair, stable score¶

How good is this model? We must not use the test set yet. And one validation split is luck-dependent (in Lesson 2, single splits ranged 78.9–81.8% on the same data).

5-fold cross-validation: cut the training data into 5 parts; train on 4, score on the 5th; rotate 5 times; average. Every customer is used for validation exactly once.

We write one helper and reuse it for every model, so all comparisons are fair (same folds, same metrics).

In [19]:
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold, cross_validate

folds = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
results = {}

def evaluate(name, model, X=X_train):
    cv = cross_validate(model, X, y_train, cv=folds,
                        scoring=('neg_root_mean_squared_error', 'neg_mean_absolute_error', 'r2'))
    results[name] = {
        'RMSE': -cv['test_neg_root_mean_squared_error'].mean(),
        'RMSE ± (spread)': cv['test_neg_root_mean_squared_error'].std(),
        'MAE': -cv['test_neg_mean_absolute_error'].mean(),
        'R²': cv['test_r2'].mean(),
    }
    return pd.DataFrame(results).T.round(3)

from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor   # scikit-learn's built-in 'predict the average' model

evaluate('0 · Baseline (mean)', DummyRegressor(strategy='mean'))
evaluate('1 · Linear regression', make_pipeline(preprocess, LinearRegression()))
Out[19]:
RMSE RMSE ± (spread) MAE R²
0 · Baseline (mean) 11,688.80 640.88 8,789.32 -0.00
1 · Linear regression 6,123.65 189.30 4,221.96 0.72

Result: linear regression cuts the typical error from ~$12,000 to ~$6,100 and explains ~72% of the variation (R² 0.72). The "±" column shows how much the score wobbles across folds; differences smaller than that are probably noise.

📘 Revision (Lesson 2): cross-validation gives a stable estimate and shows its uncertainty. Test set still locked.

Step 9 · Regularisation: does penalising weights help?¶

Ridge shrinks all weights a little; Lasso can push useless weights to exactly zero. Both fight overfitting (memorising noise). alpha = how strong the penalty is.

In [20]:
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge, Lasso

for alpha in [1, 10, 100]:
    evaluate(f'2 · Ridge alpha={alpha}', make_pipeline(preprocess, Ridge(alpha=alpha)))
for alpha in [10, 100, 500]:
    table = evaluate(f'3 · Lasso alpha={alpha}', make_pipeline(preprocess, Lasso(alpha=alpha, max_iter=50000)))
table
Out[20]:
RMSE RMSE ± (spread) MAE R²
0 · Baseline (mean) 11,688.80 640.88 8,789.32 -0.00
1 · Linear regression 6,123.65 189.30 4,221.96 0.72
2 · Ridge alpha=1 6,123.91 187.50 4,232.15 0.72
2 · Ridge alpha=10 6,156.15 180.54 4,328.13 0.72
2 · Ridge alpha=100 7,280.08 308.72 5,244.35 0.61
3 · Lasso alpha=10 6,121.87 188.20 4,220.49 0.72
3 · Lasso alpha=100 6,121.41 183.53 4,230.53 0.72
3 · Lasso alpha=500 6,299.61 238.27 4,461.45 0.71

Result: no real improvement; too much penalty (Ridge 100, Lasso 500) makes it worse.

Why? Regularisation cures overfitting. But our model has only 8 weights and ~1,000 customers; it is not overfitting. Its problem is the opposite: it is too simple (underfitting / high bias). Medicine for the wrong disease doesn't help.

📘 Revision (Lessons 2, 4): first diagnose (bias or variance?), then treat. In Lesson 4, Ridge helped a lot because that model had 29 features and overfit. Here it can't.

So how do we find what is missing? We read the model's mistakes.

Step 10 · Read the mistakes → feature engineering¶

A residual = actual − predicted. If the model were capturing everything, residuals would look like random noise with no pattern. Any pattern in the residuals is information the model missed.

In [21]:
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_predict

cv_pred = cross_val_predict(make_pipeline(preprocess, LinearRegression()), X_train, y_train, cv=folds)
residuals = y_train - cv_pred

group = np.where(train_df.smoker == 'yes', 'smoker', 'non-smoker') + np.where(train_df.bmi >= 30, ', BMI ≥ 30', ', BMI < 30')
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(16, 5))
sns.scatterplot(x=cv_pred, y=residuals, hue=group, s=22, ax=ax[0])
ax[0].axhline(0, color='black'); ax[0].set_xlabel('predicted'); ax[0].set_ylabel('residual (actual − predicted)')
ax[0].set_title('Residuals: should be random noise...')
pd.Series(residuals.values).groupby(group).mean().sort_values().plot.barh(ax=ax[1], color='darkorange')
ax[1].set_title('Average mistake per group ($)')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Not random at all! The average mistakes:

  • smokers with BMI ≥ 30: the model under-predicts by ~$8,000
  • smokers with BMI < 30: it over-predicts by ~$8,000

This is the interaction we spotted in Step 4.3. The model gives smoking one fixed bonus (~$23,000) to every smoker, but reality gives a small bonus to lean smokers and a huge one to obese smokers.

The fix: feature engineering¶

We create new columns that carry this knowledge:

  • obese = 1 if BMI ≥ 30 (a medical threshold, not something we invented)
  • smoker_obese = smoker × obese → lets the model give obese smokers their own extra charge
  • age² → lets the line curve upward for older people (Step 4.2)

It's still linear regression (linear in the weights), but now it can draw a much richer shape.

We wrap this in a function and put it inside the pipeline, so new customers get the same features automatically.

In [22]:
from sklearn.preprocessing import FunctionTransformer

def add_features(data):
    data = data.copy()
    data['smoker_yes'] = (data['smoker'] == 'yes').astype(int)
    data['obese'] = (data['bmi'] >= 30).astype(int)
    data['smoker_obese'] = data['smoker_yes'] * data['obese']
    data['age2'] = data['age'] ** 2
    return data

preprocess_fe = ColumnTransformer([
    ('num', StandardScaler(), ['age', 'age2', 'bmi', 'children']),
    ('bin', 'passthrough', ['smoker_yes', 'obese', 'smoker_obese']),
    ('cat', OneHotEncoder(drop='first', handle_unknown='ignore'), ['sex', 'region']),
])

engineered_linear = make_pipeline(FunctionTransformer(add_features), preprocess_fe, LinearRegression())
evaluate('4 · Linear + engineered features', engineered_linear)
Out[22]:
RMSE RMSE ± (spread) MAE R²
0 · Baseline (mean) 11,688.80 640.88 8,789.32 -0.00
1 · Linear regression 6,123.65 189.30 4,221.96 0.72
2 · Ridge alpha=1 6,123.91 187.50 4,232.15 0.72
2 · Ridge alpha=10 6,156.15 180.54 4,328.13 0.72
2 · Ridge alpha=100 7,280.08 308.72 5,244.35 0.61
3 · Lasso alpha=10 6,121.87 188.20 4,220.49 0.72
3 · Lasso alpha=100 6,121.41 183.53 4,230.53 0.72
3 · Lasso alpha=500 6,299.61 238.27 4,461.45 0.71
4 · Linear + engineered features 4,535.72 148.68 2,487.80 0.85

Huge jump: RMSE from ~$6,100 to ~$4,500, R² from 0.72 to 0.85, MAE nearly halved. Same algorithm, better features. No regularisation trick came close.

💡 The most important lesson of this lab: better data and features usually beat a fancier algorithm. And we found the feature by looking at the mistakes, not by guessing.

Let's read the new weights:

In [23]:
engineered_linear.fit(X_train, y_train)
names = engineered_linear[1].get_feature_names_out()
pd.Series(engineered_linear[-1].coef_, index=names).round(0).sort_values()
Out[23]:
num__age                -1,133.00
cat__region_southwest   -1,074.00
bin__obese                -631.00
cat__region_southeast     -578.00
cat__sex_male             -482.00
cat__region_northwest     -158.00
num__bmi                   510.00
num__children              882.00
num__age2                4,807.00
bin__smoker_yes         13,199.00
bin__smoker_obese       19,597.00
dtype: float64

Now smoker_obese ≈ +$19,600 on top of smoker ≈ +$13,200. So an obese smoker pays ~$33,000 extra, a lean smoker ~$13,000 extra, exactly the two red clouds in the BMI chart. (The two age weights work together to draw a curve; read them as a pair, not one by one.)

Step 11 · A decision tree: can it find the interaction by itself?¶

Trees ask yes/no questions, so they can discover "smoker AND BMI > 30" without us engineering it. Trees don't need scaling (a split only asks "is it above this value?"), so we only one-hot encode.

We tune max_depth with cross-validation, and use min_samples_leaf=10 so no leaf is based on a handful of customers.

In [24]:
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor, plot_tree

preprocess_tree = ColumnTransformer([
    ('num', 'passthrough', numeric_cols),
    ('cat', OneHotEncoder(drop='first', handle_unknown='ignore'), categorical_cols),
])

for depth in [2, 3, 4, 5, 8, None]:
    table = evaluate(f'5 · Tree depth={depth}', make_pipeline(preprocess_tree, DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=depth, min_samples_leaf=10, random_state=0)))
table.tail(6)
Out[24]:
RMSE RMSE ± (spread) MAE R²
5 · Tree depth=2 5,193.05 221.08 3,470.69 0.80
5 · Tree depth=3 4,866.37 196.37 2,916.59 0.82
5 · Tree depth=4 4,725.60 189.82 2,698.38 0.83
5 · Tree depth=5 4,722.70 203.94 2,700.43 0.83
5 · Tree depth=8 4,912.69 199.12 2,823.31 0.82
5 · Tree depth=None 4,892.22 189.66 2,803.69 0.82

Best depth is about 4 (RMSE ~$4,700). Deeper trees start memorising (Lesson 2's U-shape again). Let's look at a depth-3 tree, the most explainable model in ML:

In [25]:
small_tree = make_pipeline(preprocess_tree, DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3, min_samples_leaf=10, random_state=0)).fit(X_train, y_train)
plt.figure(figsize=(20, 7))
plot_tree(small_tree[-1], feature_names=[n.split('__')[1] for n in small_tree[0].get_feature_names_out()],
          filled=True, rounded=True, impurity=False, fontsize=12, precision=0)
plt.show()

The tree discovered our interaction on its own: first question smoker?; for smokers, the next question is BMI ≤ 30?, which splits ~$20,000 apart. For non-smokers it asks about age instead. That's the same story our residuals told.

📘 Revision (Lesson 5): trees find interactions automatically and are readable, but alone they predict in steps (a staircase) and are unstable.

Step 12 · Ensembles: random forest and gradient boosting¶

  • Random forest: average hundreds of different deep trees → stable (fixes variance).
  • Gradient boosting: add small trees one by one, each fixing the remaining mistakes (fixes bias).
In [26]:
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor, HistGradientBoostingRegressor, GradientBoostingRegressor

evaluate('6 · Random forest', make_pipeline(preprocess_tree, RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1)))
evaluate('7 · Gradient boosting (tuned)', make_pipeline(preprocess_tree, GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=200, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=3, random_state=0)))
table = evaluate('8 · HistGradientBoosting', make_pipeline(preprocess_tree, HistGradientBoostingRegressor(learning_rate=0.05, max_iter=200, max_depth=3, random_state=0)))
table.sort_values('RMSE')
Out[26]:
RMSE RMSE ± (spread) MAE R²

Surprise? The ensembles land around $4,600–4,700: much better than plain linear regression, but not better than our engineered linear model (~$4,500), and the difference is within the ± spread.

Why? This problem has one main hidden interaction (smoker × obese) and a smooth age curve. Once we hand those to linear regression, there is little left for trees to discover. Boosting shines when there are many interactions nobody can find by hand (Lesson 6: "boosting wins big on large, messy data").

📘 Revision (Lesson 6): always compare against a strong simple model. Complexity must earn its place.

Step 13 · Which error metric? A log-target experiment¶

Charges are skewed (Step 2). A common trick: predict log(charges) instead, then convert back with exp. Let's test it instead of trusting it.

In [27]:
from sklearn.compose import TransformedTargetRegressor

log_model = TransformedTargetRegressor(regressor=make_pipeline(FunctionTransformer(add_features), preprocess_fe, LinearRegression()),
                                       func=np.log, inverse_func=np.exp)
evaluate('9 · Engineered linear, log target', log_model).loc[['4 · Linear + engineered features', '9 · Engineered linear, log target']]
Out[27]:
RMSE RMSE ± (spread) MAE R²
4 · Linear + engineered features 4,535.72 148.68 2,487.80 0.85
9 · Engineered linear, log target 8,826.32 1,307.54 4,221.90 0.43

Much worse in RMSE. Why? Predicting log(charges) makes the model care about percentage errors equally for cheap and expensive customers. Being 20% off on a $2,000 customer counts the same as 20% off on a $40,000 customer. But RMSE in dollars is dominated by expensive customers, exactly the ones the log model now cares less about.

Lesson: a trick is only "good" relative to the metric that matters to the business. For pricing in dollars, RMSE/MAE in dollars → no log. If the business cared about relative error, the log version could win.

📘 Revision (Lesson 3): the metric must match the business cost, just as we chose the churn threshold from the cost of a call vs a lost customer.

Decision¶

The top models are within noise of each other. Tie-breakers come from the business:

  • Explainability is a legal requirement → the engineered linear model is a formula anyone can audit; boosting needs extra tools.
  • Simpler model → easier to maintain, faster, fewer surprises.

Winner: 4 · Linear + engineered features. Now, and only now, we unlock the test set.

In [29]:
final_model = make_pipeline(FunctionTransformer(add_features), preprocess_fe, LinearRegression())
final_model.fit(X_train, y_train)          # train on ALL training data

X_test, y_test = test_df.drop(columns='charges'), test_df.charges
test_pred = final_model.predict(X_test)

print(f'TEST RMSE: ${rmse(y_test, test_pred):,.0f}')
print(f'TEST MAE:  ${mean_absolute_error(y_test, test_pred):,.0f}')
print(f'TEST R²:   {r2_score(y_test, test_pred):.3f}')
print(f'(Baseline on the same test set: RMSE ${rmse(y_test, np.full(len(y_test), y_train.mean())):,.0f})')

TEST RMSE: $4,158
TEST MAE:  $2,394
TEST R²:   0.906
(Baseline on the same test set: RMSE $13,612)

Test result is in line with cross-validation (even slightly better: normal luck of a 268-customer test set), so our CV estimate was honest. Test RMSE ~$4,200 vs ~$13,600 for the baseline; the plain average miss (MAE) is ~$2,400.

Where are the remaining errors? Let's look:

In [30]:
plt.scatter(y_test, test_pred, s=18, alpha=.7)
lim = [0, 65000]; plt.plot(lim, lim, 'k--', label='perfect prediction')
plt.xlabel('actual charges'); plt.ylabel('predicted charges'); plt.legend(); plt.title('Test set: predicted vs actual'); plt.show()

Most points hug the diagonal. Every big miss (21 customers off by more than $5,000) is an under-prediction, and most of them are non-smokers from the "middle band" of Step 4.2. Something made them expensive (an illness, an accident) that is not in our data.

No algorithm can find information that isn't there. To do better, the business would need new features (e.g. medical history), not a new model.

Step 15 · Explain a prediction (the regulator's question)¶

"Why does this customer get this estimate?" With a linear model the answer is exact: prediction = base + sum of (weight × feature). Let's explain one test customer. (Note: numeric features are scaled, so a below-average age gives a negative contribution.)

In [31]:
customer = X_test[X_test.smoker == 'yes'].iloc[[0]]   # pick a smoker: a more interesting explanation
display(customer)

transformed = final_model[:-1].transform(customer)
names = [n.split('__')[1] for n in final_model[1].get_feature_names_out()]
contrib = pd.Series(transformed[0] * final_model[-1].coef_, index=names)

print(f'Base: ${final_model[-1].intercept_:,.0f}  (a non-smoking, non-obese woman in the northeast with average age, BMI and children)')
print(contrib.round(0).sort_values(key=abs, ascending=False).to_string())
print(f'Prediction: ${final_model[-1].intercept_ + contrib.sum():,.0f}   (model says ${final_model.predict(customer)[0]:,.0f})')

Model-agnostic check: permutation importance (Lesson 5). Shuffle one input column on the test set and see how much RMSE gets worse. Big increase = important.

In [32]:
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance

perm = permutation_importance(final_model, X_test, y_test, scoring='neg_root_mean_squared_error', n_repeats=20, random_state=0)
pd.Series(perm.importances_mean, index=X_test.columns).sort_values().plot.barh(color='seagreen')
plt.xlabel('RMSE increase when shuffled ($)'); plt.title('Permutation importance (test set)'); plt.show()

Smoking dominates (shuffling it adds ~$12,600 of error), then BMI (~$3,800, mostly through the obese-smoker effect) and age (~$2,700). Sex and region add almost nothing (under $60): candidates for removal in a simpler model.

Step 16 · Save the model and use it like a product¶

In a company, the model leaves the notebook. We save the whole pipeline (feature engineering + encoding + scaling + model) as one file. Then any app can load it and price a new customer from raw inputs.

In [33]:
import joblib

joblib.dump(final_model, 'charges_model.joblib')
print('Saved. File size:', os.path.getsize('charges_model.joblib'), 'bytes')

# later, in another program (an API, a web app, a batch job):
loaded = joblib.load('charges_model.joblib')

def estimate_charges(age, sex, bmi, children, smoker, region):
    row = pd.DataFrame([dict(age=age, sex=sex, bmi=bmi, children=children, smoker=smoker, region=region)])
    return float(loaded.predict(row)[0])

for person in [(30, 'female', 24.0, 1, 'no', 'northeast'),
               (30, 'female', 24.0, 1, 'yes', 'northeast'),
               (30, 'female', 34.0, 1, 'yes', 'northeast')]:
    print(person, '→', f'${estimate_charges(*person):,.0f}')

Saved. File size: 4801 bytes
(30, 'female', 24.0, 1, 'no', 'northeast') → $6,030
(30, 'female', 24.0, 1, 'yes', 'northeast') → $19,229
(30, 'female', 34.0, 1, 'yes', 'northeast') → $39,038

Look at the three people: identical except smoking and BMI. Smoking adds ~$13,000; smoking and obesity adds ~$33,000. The model's behaviour matches what we discovered, which is exactly what a reviewer wants to see.

Production checklist (what would come next in a company):

  • Input validation: reject age 250 or region "mars" before predicting.
  • Monitoring / drift (Lesson 2): if new customers start to look different (e.g. many more smokers), the model's errors change; track them and retrain.
  • Versioning: save which data and code produced each model file.
  • Fairness review: sex contributes little here; a company might drop it deliberately for fairness reasons.

Step 17 · Summary: the whole course in one lab¶

Step Concept Lesson
Problem framing, supervised regression what ML is 1
Removed a duplicate, split first, test used once leakage, honest evaluation 2
Cross-validation with spread (±) stable estimates 2
Baseline first metrics, always compare 3
Metric must match the business (log-target experiment) choosing metrics 3
Loss + gradient descent + direct formula how models learn 4
Scaling, one-hot encoding, pipelines preprocessing 4
Ridge / Lasso did not help → diagnose bias vs variance regularisation 4
Residuals → feature engineering (the biggest win) underfitting, features 2, 4
Tree found the interaction itself decision trees 5
Forest / boosting ≈ engineered linear ensembles, complexity must earn its place 6
Spotting groups in charts unsupervised thinking 7
Explaining predictions, saving the pipeline production —

The 6-step recipe you can apply to any problem¶

  1. Frame the problem and the business metric.
  2. Split first; lock the test set.
  3. Explore training data; ask "what should I do about this?"
  4. Baseline, then a simple model in a pipeline, scored with cross-validation.
  5. Read the mistakes → better features → stronger models only if they earn it.
  6. Test once, explain, save, monitor.

Exercises¶

  1. Remove sex and region. Does cross-validated RMSE change? What would you tell the business?
  2. Add age × smoker as another feature. Does it help? Why might it?
  3. Train an SGDRegressor (gradient descent inside scikit-learn) in the same pipeline. Compare with LinearRegression.
  4. Use MAE instead of RMSE to pick the winner. Does the winner change?
  5. Build the leaderboard again with random_state=7 for the folds. Which conclusions stay the same?

Data: "Medical Cost Personal Datasets" (Machine Learning with R, Brett Lantz; via stedy/Machine-Learning-with-R-datasets). Lab structure inspired by Jovian's "Linear Regression with Scikit-learn". Book background (optional): Géron, Hands-On Machine Learning, Ch 2 & 4.
